narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which

This is Dirk dance. 1841.

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dirk dance originated in Scotland as a traditional weapon dance, with research suggesting it may have started as a series of physical movements intended for training in the use of the dirk.
Records confirm that a Dirk Dance was featured in Highland Dance competitions by 1841.
It was also performed alongside other weapons such as the Lochaber axe, broadsword, flail, and paired targe and dirk.
on_screen: Map: Scotland · Europe
Image — MISSING

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Included in historical Highland Dance competitions and served as a combative training method.
A lost two-dancer tradition featured a dramatic narrative of killing and resurrection.
Today it is a revived tradition.
on_screen: Footage: The Highland Dirk Dance From Mary Isdale MacNab (https://archive.org/details/TheHighlandDirkDanceFromMaryIsdaleMacNab)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is performed as a solo or by two or more people dancing in unison while brandishing a dirk.
The style imitates combat, featuring knife techniques combined with wrestling-style kicks, trips, and sweeps, bearing resemblance to combative forms like Pentjak Silat.
Watch for combat imitation and knife techniques.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key figures include J. F. and T. M. Flett (researchers), Mary Isdale Mac Nab of Vancouver, D.C. Mather (Scottish piping and dance champion), the MacLennan brothers, and Mona Douglas (Manx folk researcher).

Includes the Highland Dirk Dance, a version utilizing single-sticks and targe shields performed by the MacLennan brothers, a two-person narrative version with a resurrection theme, and a Manx variant involving a dagger recovered by Mona Douglas.
Connected to broader Scottish Highland dancing traditions and historical combat training methods, with stylistic parallels noted to martial arts like Pentjak Silat.

music_brief.purpose: original soundtrack faithful to the tradition, with documented commercial reuse rights and no recurring royalties
music_brief.rights_rule: A composition brief does not clear an output. Record the provider/model/version, terms and date, input rights, output licence, restrictions and review before release.
music_brief.prompt: Original instrumental composition in the musical world of Dirk dance (Scotland). Instruments: pipes. Mood: combative, martial, vigorous. New melody, new arrangement: do not quote or imitate any specific recorded song; keep the idiom, the instruments, the pulse and the proportions.

tracks.use: chapters: dance it to the music

rules: Original composition only — no sampling, no melody of any existing recording, no lyrics from any song.
Traditional public-domain tunes may be used only when the profile names them and a public-domain source is on file; otherwise compose new material in the idiom.
Keep the proportions true: the meter, the tempo range and the instrument roles the sources describe.
Label every generated track with the tool, the date and this brief, so provenance is always clear.
